cards.title: Each tablet keeps its own list of claimed tokens
cards.atAShow: A GM deletes a transaction. The engine frees the token, but every tablet that stays connected keeps refusing it as already scanned until someone reloads. A tablet that drops its connection during Reset All Scores comes back still holding the old claims, and refuses tokens the engine has cleared.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine decides which tokens are claimed, but each tablet holds a copy that only grows: added on scan, merged on reconnect, removed only when a scan fails. The engine's own messages also skip facts changed by another path, such as a team created by a scan.
cards.designTerms: The engine's transaction service should own the claimed-token fact; tablets should hold only its copy. Today the tablet's networked storage module updates its copy through one hand-wired handler per message, so the seam leaks: any path without a handler leaves the copy stale. No locality.

cards.title: Service health and service state travel on separate paths
cards.atAShow: If Home Assistant or MPD is down when the engine starts, the lighting and music panels stay disabled until someone reloads the tablet. If MPD dies mid-show, the health row turns red alone while the music card keeps its playing look and the progress bar keeps moving. A volume change on one tablet's audio panel never reaches the other tablets' sliders.
cards.whyItHappens: Each venue service keeps two facts: its health in a central registry and its own state in its own record. The engine pushes the health row when health changes, and pushes a service's state only on a hand-written list of that service's events. An outage is on no list.
cards.designTerms: Each service module should own one record carrying health and state. Today the seam leaks: the broadcast module re-implements each service's change set as a per-domain event list, so the interface callers must know is the full event list, and locality is lost.

cards.title: Engine trusts its stale picture of outside programs
cards.atAShow: A video stayed stopped for about 28 seconds because the parser held each player message until the next one arrived. A false video finished can fire two seconds in, flipping the display back and restoring music. When MPD dies the engine still says playing and the controls stay dead until the next 15-second sweep. A cue with a 2-second video never completes.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine learns what VLC, MPD and the other programs are doing by parsing their text or event streams into a cached copy that starts from a default and carries no age. Re-reads are partial, and the video queue, cue timelines and health rows treat the copy as the program.
cards.designTerms: A reader module per outside program should own the engine's picture of it, behind one interface: read, stream, resync, last-read time. Today the seam leaks: the video queue, cue timeline and health rows read each service's ageless cache directly, so locality is lost.

cards.title: Nothing says what a game boundary clears or keeps
cards.atAShow: The GM ends the game and restarts the engine; the ended game comes back as the current one and player scans keep landing in it. When the game ends, a tablet that reconnects loses its history and the wall scoreboard goes blank. A once-only cue spent in game one stays spent in game two.
cards.whyItHappens: Game start, end, reset, engine restart, tablet reload and reconnect each have their own code in each component. No table says, per fact and copy, whether a boundary clears, keeps or re-fetches it, and no message announces a boundary; screens infer one from a changed session id.
cards.designTerms: A boundary-table module should own each fact's lifetime at a game boundary: clear, keep or re-fetch. No such interface exists, so the session, cue-engine, reset and tablet modules each encode their own cases; the seam leaks and one boundary change has no locality.

cards.title: Boot and Reset System wire the engine differently
cards.atAShow: The GM presses Reset System to recover mid-show. The music panel goes dead until someone restarts the engine. Later, Reset All Scores sends every tablet and the TV the old transaction list, so cleared evidence comes back on the wall. The cue engine now hears each video and clock event twice, and the Display row stays red until Check Now.
cards.whyItHappens: Starting the engine and rebuilding it after a reset are two separate hand-written lists. Boot wires the storage listeners first, then the broadcasts, with one set of services; the reset wires them the other way round with a shorter set, and adds some listeners a second time.
cards.designTerms: An engine-assembly module should own which services exist, their listeners and the order they are wired. Today boot and reset each implement that by hand, so every caller knows every service and the ordering rule: the seam leaks and a change has no locality.

cards.title: Reconnect snapshot and live update are built apart
cards.atAShow: A GM reloads a tablet mid-game. The History badge stays hidden until the next scan, and a rebuilt admin panel can show the clock as --:-- until the next change. The device list flips between everyone ever and connected only, depending on which message came last.
cards.whyItHappens: For each fact the engine has one builder for the connect snapshot and another for the live message, and six places send the snapshot with hand-picked arguments. The tablet applies each by a different rule, and the restore path fires none of the events screens listen for.
cards.designTerms: Each fact's engine module should own one description of itself, serving snapshot and live push alike. The snapshot builder is shallow: its interface is a hand-passed list of every module, and five tablet adapters reshape its output, so the seam leaks both ways.

cards.title: A reply never says which request, final or stored
cards.atAShow: Player devices upload their queued scans while no game exists. The engine answers processed, stores nothing, and both devices delete the scans. A GM's scan that can never succeed comes back as a generic error, so the tablet replays it at every reconnect with a toast each time. A slow Reset System reports failure and the new game is skipped.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine answers before or without the write that makes the fact true, calls an unstored batch processed, returns some failures as a typed result and others as a generic error, and acknowledges commands by action name alone. Each device then decides for itself what a reply means.
cards.designTerms: One commit module in the engine should own each request's outcome: which request, final or not, stored or not. That interface is split between typed results, generic errors and action-name acks, so the seam leaks and three clients each keep their own reply rule.

A system reset slower than the tablet's five-second wait reports failure, and the follow-on create session is skipped.
A command ack carries only action, success and message, so two presses of one action resolve on the first reply.

cards.title: Engine and tests both assume they own the machine
cards.atAShow: On 2026-09-15 a unit test killed the live show's video player on blue's tree. In this tree the same run kills the live engine's VLC signal monitor and overwrites its process files. A killed engine leaves a full-screen player behind. Twenty-one test suites open a browser on the show TV. The operator's health script says VLC not found while the player runs.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine names and ends its helper programs by fixed file names and by command-line patterns over the whole machine, written as the only engine on the box. The test layers adopt whatever display, sound server and Bluetooth exist; that a layer is safe is claimed in comments, never checked.
cards.designTerms: A runtime-identity module should own which processes, files and windows belong to this engine instance. Today no such seam exists: each service module hard-codes a shared process file, and the kiosk and sound-server modules kill by machine-wide pattern, so identity has no locality.

cards.title: Tablets and phones decide facts the engine owns
cards.atAShow: A GM scans a token; the result screen says Transaction Complete with points the tablet worked out itself, before the engine has answered. The engine may refuse, and the correction arrives as a small toast. In standalone mode the tablet is the only judge, and its rules have gaps: a scan into a paused game shows complete and records nothing. A phone says revisited for last week's token.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine is the authority for scoring, claims and the scan gate, but the tablet carries its own copy of those rules, kept in step by hand and by comment, and the player devices pick their own team and their own new-or-seen. Each device shows its own verdict first.
cards.designTerms: The engine's game-rules module should own scoring, group completion and duplicate rules behind one interface both sides load. Today the tablet holds a second implementation kept in step by comment, so the seam leaks verdicts: a rule change lands in two places, with no locality.

cards.title: Screens show a normal value when nothing is known
cards.atAShow: The venue profile fails to load; six services turn not installed, no video plays, no light cue fires, and the panel reads a calm green 3 of 9. The GM presses Check Now on a down service and nothing visibly happens. The engine dies; the TV keeps counting down. The music card goes grey with no offline line, and nobody at the venue notices.
cards.whyItHappens: No fact on the wire says whether it is known, unknown, stale or partial. Snapshot builders catch errors and send plausible defaults, a missing profile reads as no equipment, healthy means a program answered, and the check times that exist are never shown. The screen draws a normal value.
cards.designTerms: The health registry should own whether each service fact is known, unknown or stale, and when it was seen. Today the pushed facts' interface carries neither, so snapshot builders turn errors into defaults and the seam leaks: a failure crosses as a normal value.

cards.title: Several places answer the same question, each differently
cards.atAShow: Is a video playing has eight answers. A paused video counts as free, so a player is told their video was triggered while it waits, and releasing a held video plays over the paused one. Release All can stop at the first refused video. Music stays ducked after the queue is cleared. The downloaded report's two totals disagree.
cards.whyItHappens: Questions such as is a video playing, which teams exist and may the GM scan now are answered by several functions or stored values, each with its own rule and write path, so they disagree at the edges. No rule says which answerer every reader must use.
cards.designTerms: One resolver module per question should own the verdict behind a one-call interface. Today there is no such seam: the queue, the command gate and the ducking count each implement 'is a video playing' by their own rule, so that knowledge has no locality.

examples.text: Seven of those answers are in the video code; a paused video counts as not playing for four of them.
Held cues and held videos live in two stores; Release All can stop at the first refused video.
Ducking keeps its own count of playing videos; music stays ducked after the queue is cleared.
The GM's permission to scan is read from a local copy; after a reload it blocks scans in an active game until the first snapshot arrives.
Which teams exist has several answers; a second GM adding the same name gets an error though the team exists.
The downloaded report has two different final totals per team: the timeline leaves out group bonuses, the standings include them.

cards.title: Pack edits reach each part of the kit differently
cards.atAShow: A designer publishes a pack change and does not restart. The TV shows evidence by the new rules while the engine scores by the old. The file the engine serves no longer matches the hash in its own manifest, so a scanner that checks rejects it. A tablet running a different pack is only written to the log; nothing tells the GM. The publish tells the running engine nothing.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine freezes one pack at start, yet its file endpoints serve whatever is on disk and its token endpoint re-reads every call. The TV, tablet and hardware scanner each load it at their own moment and keep it; the phone reads its own copy. No message says it changed.
cards.designTerms: The pack service should own one versioned pack view. Its interface leaks the disk: it checks a path against the frozen inventory, then serves live bytes, and the token service re-reads the file around it, so frozen and live state cross the seam. No locality.

examples.text: After a pack edit with no restart, endpoints serve new bytes while the engine scores from the old pack; hash mismatches.
Publishing a pack from the config tool tells the running engine nothing; the engine scores by the edit only after a restart.
A tablet or scanner on a different pack than the engine is only logged; nothing tells the device or GM.
Before a restart the TV shows evidence by the new rules while the engine scores by the old.
A new pack reaches a hardware scanner only after a reboot; tokens cannot be re-synced by command.
A password changed in the tool's env editor works at once on the tool, only after restart on the engine.

cards.title: The engine does not know who is connected
cards.atAShow: A tablet loses Wi-Fi and reloads; the engine still holds its old socket under the same station name and refuses the new one for up to about 85 seconds. Two tablets started together pick the same station name from an open list. The TV joins the GM room, receives every transaction and all ten service domains, and filters on its own side.
cards.whyItHappens: Whether a credential is asked for, and what a station is called, comes from a word the device sends or a route's default. Every socket event and route checks separately; none says who its audience is, so every socket gets everything and reads need no login.
cards.designTerms: A role-table module should own who each connection is and what it may receive. Today the handshake seam leaks: it trusts a self-declared word, and each route and socket event checks on its own, so access rules have no locality.

examples.text: Anyone on the kit network fetches the whole game state; a socket claiming not to be a GM gets it too.
The TV sits in the GM room, receives every transaction and all ten service domains, and filters on its own side.
Two tablets reading the open name list before connecting pick the same station name; the second is refused.
A tablet that reloads after losing Wi-Fi cannot replace its own stale socket for up to about 85 seconds.
An ESP32 is listed as a web player scanner because its health poll sends no type.
Displays get no device record and share one id, so the engine cannot count connected TVs.

cards.title: Names joining two places are kept by hand
cards.atAShow: A GM opens Team Details: the score box is wrong, GM adjustments never appear, completed groups read In Progress with a $0 bonus, while the scoreboard screen on the same tablet shows the real total. Game Activity shows Unknown, no stars, $0 for a token no player scanned first. The video Playing badge never appears, because its element was never in the page.
cards.whyItHappens: A screen reads a property the object lacks; a renderer looks up an element the page never had; a module listens for an event nothing sends; the contract lists events nobody emits. Each name is written on both sides, and a wrong side yields nothing instead of an error.
cards.designTerms: A join-check module should own every name two modules share, so a missing side fails at load. Today the facade-strategy seam leaks: Team Details reads a field only the strategy adapter holds, the facade never exposes it, and the miss is silent.

examples.text: Team Details reads a field the facade lacks and a method no strategy defines; wrong score, groups always In Progress.
Game Activity reads token fields off the lookup's wrapper, so a GM-claimed token shows Unknown, no stars, $0.
The video Playing, Paused, Idle badge never renders: its element was never in the page.
The cue timeline waits for a skipped field nothing sends and correlates videos by a field the pack lacks.
The contract lists events nobody sends, misses ones the engine emits, and disagrees with itself on the music push.

cards.title: The deployed game is many parts nothing compares
cards.atAShow: Between shows, a rollback moves the parent checkout but no submodule backwards, and pm2 restart keeps serving the pre-rollback scanner build, so a bad rollback reaches the next show. A machine built from the tree's own documents pairs a speaker that connects with no audio profile, because the documents carry the wrong Bluetooth role.
cards.whyItHappens: The show machine is a parent checkout, four submodules on main, a scanner build folder, hand-copied media, host rules, hooks and program names fixed to one OS release. Each part moves by its own hand-run step and nothing compares them afterwards, so a half-applied change goes unnoticed.
cards.designTerms: A deploy-check module should own what is installed: pack hash, scanner build id, submodule pins, behind one boot-time interface. Today no module owns it: each part is moved by its own hand-run step, so the seam between source and running machine leaks unchecked.

examples.text: Rolling back with git submodule update --force moves no submodule backwards under the merge setting.
pm2 restart skips the build, so the GM scanner keeps serving the pre-rollback code.
The tree's own documents give the Bluetooth role blue found wrong, so a new machine pairs a silent speaker.
The token sync cannot carry media; copied by hand first, or tokens point at nothing.
Program names and install commands are fixed to one OS release; a new machine logs warnings or refuses pip.
The ESP32 checks no certificate at all, because the kit's self-signed certificate is pinned and distributed nowhere.

cards.seenLive: Blue hit a half-applied rollback, a pre-rollback scanner build after pm2 restart, and a speaker with no audio profile.

cards.title: A green test run proves nothing about the show
cards.atAShow: Nothing shows at the show; this is why the other fifteen reached one. Unit tests stayed green while Team Details showed the wrong score, because their fake facade had the field the real one lacks. A delete step in an end-to-end flow had been silently skipping on a selector that never matched. Blue's last full run skipped 62 tests, and group completion has no test on real content.
cards.whyItHappens: Fakes are written by hand with nothing comparing them to the real classes. Steps that find no element, or check only that no error appeared, pass. Every test engine runs under a flag that changes what Reset System does, so no layer runs the reset the show runs.
cards.designTerms: A test's fake is an adapter, so the real class should own its shape and the fake must satisfy that interface. Today each fake is hand-written and checked against nothing; the seam leaks, and no test crosses one path from authority to screen.

examples.text: Unit-test fakes drifted from the real classes, so tests stayed green while Team Details and Game Activity were wrong.
A page-object selector never matched the Team Details cards, so a delete step had been silently skipping.
Blue's last full run skipped 62 tests; group completion has no end-to-end test on real content.
The listener registry removes listeners only under the test flag, so no layer runs the Reset System the show runs.
Not one screen image is checked in either end-to-end suite; no baseline exists to compare against.
Parent CI never runs several suites; the config tool's own workflow never runs from this repository.
